summary: Describes the state of the Internet from an architectural viewpoint, concentrating on end-to-end connectivity and transparency, and what happens when things like firewalls and translators break them. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2775 explains what the Internet loses when devices in the middle change or restrict traffic. It describes how those changes affect applications, security, and possible network-layer futures.

questions: what is the end to end principle
how does nat break end to end connectivity
how can nat affect end-to-end connectivity
subtitle: An architectural look at how intermediaries affect end-to-end connectivity and addressing.

tldr.problem: The Internet's original design let packets travel between endpoints with one universal addressing scheme, but several network practices were reducing that transparency.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the end-to-end argument, lists causes and effects of lost transparency, and sketches three possible futures involving IPv6.
tldr.outcome: It makes no recommendations. Its conclusion says partial IPv6 deployment is messy but avoids the dead ends described for paths without IPv6.

today: RFC 2775 is an Informational memo published in February 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes the Internet's architecture at that time and makes no recommendations.

sections.title: What Internet Transparency Means
sections.content:
This Informational memo examines end-to-end connectivity at the Internet network layer. It uses transparency to mean a single logical addressing scheme and packets that travel from source to destination essentially unaltered.

The document was prepared as input to an IAB workshop in July 1999. It says it is not complete or definitive, makes no recommendations, and does not discuss routing implications, quality-of-service router state, or namespace issues in depth.
sections.plainLanguage: Transparency means that endpoints can address each other using one Internet-wide scheme and send packets without extensive changes in the middle. The memo describes how that design was changing.

sections.title: Three Aspects of End-to-End Design
sections.content:
The end-to-end argument says some functions can only be performed correctly by the endpoints, so network state should not be required for those functions. The memo also discusses end-to-end performance, including how network behavior interacts with transport protocols.

Address transparency means that source and destination addresses act as stable identifiers and packets move essentially unchanged. The memo notes that applications and protocols have incorporated addresses into checksums, signatures, and other data, so changing address behavior can affect them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some communication tasks must be checked by the programs at each end. The network should carry packets, while applications handle the tasks that require their knowledge.

sections.title: What Reduces Transparency
sections.content:
The memo lists Intranets, dynamically assigned addresses, firewalls, private addresses, network address translators (NATs), gateways, relays, proxies, caches, split DNS, and load-sharing techniques as causes of reduced transparency. Some are intentional controls; others arose as responses to address limitations or operational needs.

NATs can break applications that carry IP addresses in their own messages unless an application-level gateway or proxy adapts them. A firewall or proxy can also limit which traffic crosses a network boundary or change which endpoint a remote server sees.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls, address translators, and proxies can block or change traffic between endpoints. They can be useful, but applications may need special handling when addresses or connections change.

sections.title: Effects on Applications and Security
sections.content:
The memo says the listed mechanisms were in widespread use but their extent could not be measured reliably. It identifies costs in administration, configuration, and fault diagnosis. Intermediaries that hold connection state can also become single points of failure.

The memo describes effects on end-to-end IPsec and on mechanisms such as DNSSEC and Kerberos that rely on address values. It also notes that dynamic client addresses favor client-server designs over peer-to-peer applications and complicate stable access to mobile servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Changes to addresses can break security mechanisms and applications that depend on them. Intermediaries also add state and configuration that can make failures harder to diagnose.

sections.title: Possible IPv6 Futures
sections.content:
The memo outlines three scenarios: successful migration to IPv6, complete failure of IPv6, and partial IPv6 deployment. In the successful-migration scenario, the larger address space could restore address transparency, while firewalls and Intranets would remain. In the failure scenario, the memo considers address reallocation and eventual fragmentation.

The conclusion says none of the scenarios is simple. It describes partial IPv6 deployment as a necessary step toward full deployment and as a path that avoids the dead ends of the non-IPv6 scenarios. These are scenarios, not recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo compares full, failed, and partial IPv6 deployment. It says partial deployment is difficult but avoids the dead ends it describes for futures without IPv6.

viz.caption: THE THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES DESCRIBED IN RFC 2775

items.title: Successful IPv6 migration
items.text: Address transparency could be restored; Intranets and firewalls remain.

items.title: Complete IPv6 failure
items.text: The memo describes continued workarounds and possible network fragmentation.

items.title: Partial IPv6 deployment
items.text: IPv4 and IPv6 coexist, with transition techniques becoming ongoing features.
